Broughtest
BRAWT-est
v.t. (2nd pers. sing.)
The archaic second person singular past of bring, from Anglo-Saxon bringan with the -est ending. Webster 1828 records the form as the second person of the preterit. In Scripture it is nearly always addressed to God about the exodus — and once, damningly, to Moses.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The form belongs to direct address, and in Scripture the One usually addressed is God about His deliverance of Israel. Nehemiah’s great prayer of national confession begins with it: Thou art the LORD the God, who didst choose Abram, and broughtest him forth out of Ur of the Chaldees, and gavest him the name of Abraham (Nehemiah 9:7). The psalmist uses it to name an outcome after an ordeal: Thou hast caused men to ride over our heads; we went through fire and through water: but thou broughtest us out into a wealthy place (Psalm 66:12) — through, not around. Moses uses it in intercession, arguing from God’s reputation among the nations: Lest the land whence thou broughtest us out say, Because the LORD was not able to bring them into the land which he promised them (Deuteronomy 9:28). And at the calf God uses the word against Moses, disowning the people by handing them to him: Go, get thee down; for thy people, which thou broughtest out of the land of Egypt, have corrupted themselves (Exodus 32:7) — thy people, whom thou broughtest out, and Moses spends the rest of the chapter giving them back.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 records BROUGHTEST as the second person singular of the preterit of BRING — to bear, convey, or lead from a distant place to one nearer.

expand to see more

BRING, v.t. — To fetch; to bear, convey or lead from a distant to a nearer place.

To produce; to procure as a cause; to draw to.

To cause to come; to induce to a particular state or condition.

BROUGHT, pret. and pp. — of BRING.

BROUGHTEST, the second person singular of the preterit, used in direct address; now archaic.

Key Scripture

Nehemiah 9:7 — "Thou art the LORD the God, who didst choose Abram, and broughtest him forth out of Ur of the Chaldees, and gavest him the name of Abraham;"

Psalm 66:12 — "Thou hast caused men to ride over our heads; we went through fire and through water: but thou broughtest us out into a wealthy place."

Deuteronomy 9:28 — "Lest the land whence thou broughtest us out say, Because the LORD was not able to bring them into the land which he promised them, and because he hated them, he hath brought them out to slay them in the wilderness."

Exodus 32:7 — "And the LORD said unto Moses, Go, get thee down; for thy people, which thou broughtest out of the land of Egypt, have corrupted themselves:"

Modern Corruption

The archaic second person singular preserves a distinction modern English has lost — thou to one, ye to many — and its loss flattens a great deal of Scripture, including whom exactly Christ is addressing.

expand to see more

Broughtest is a second person singular form, and the Authorized Version’s pronouns are precise where modern English cannot be: thou, thee, thy, thine are always singular; ye, you, your are always plural. This is not archaism for its own sake but preserved information. When our Lord tells Peter Satan hath desired to have you (plural, all the disciples) but I have prayed for thee (singular, Peter alone), Luke 22:31-32 carries a distinction that collapses in a modern rendering. The same applies to Exodus 32:7, where God says thy people whom thou broughtest out, singling Moses out. This dictionary is not KJV-only and acknowledges other faithful translations; but the pronoun system is a real advantage of the Authorized Version, and readers who dismiss it as mere quaintness are giving up data.

Exodus 32:7 is one of the most searching moments in the Pentateuch. God calls Israel thy people, which thou broughtest out — language that hands them to Moses and disowns them — and offers to make of Moses a great nation instead. Moses refuses the offer and argues back, on two grounds: the Egyptians will say God brought them out to slay them, and God swore by Himself to Abraham, Isaac and Israel. He pleads God’s reputation and God’s oath, not Israel’s merit, of which there was none that morning. This is the pattern of biblical intercession, and it is the pattern of a greater Mediator: Christ does not plead our worthiness but His own finished work, and the ground of our standing is the covenant God swore with Himself.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yatsa (H3318) in the hiphil, to bring out; alah (H5927) in the hiphil, to bring up; the -est ending marks the second person singular in Early Modern English.

expand to see more

Hebrew yatsa (H3318), hiphil — to cause to go out, to bring forth; the standing exodus verb (Exodus 32:7; Deuteronomy 9:28).

Hebrew alah (H5927), hiphil — to bring up; used interchangeably of the deliverance from Egypt.

Hebrew Ur Kasdim — Ur of the Chaldees, whence Abram was brought (Nehemiah 9:7).

Hebrew revayah (H7310) — abundance, a place of overflow; a wealthy place (Psalm 66:12).

English -est — the second person singular ending, matching the singular pronoun thou.

Usage

"Broughtest him forth out of Ur of the Chaldees (Nehemiah 9:7) — national confession beginning with God’s election of one man."

"We went through fire and through water: but thou broughtest us out into a wealthy place (Psalm 66:12) — through, not around."

"Thy people, which thou broughtest out of the land of Egypt (Exodus 32:7) — God handing Israel to Moses, and Moses handing them back."
